testimony.committee: Board of Indian Commissioners / Office of Indian Affairs
testimony.subject: Issuance of patents-in-fee; outcomes for Indian allottees
testimony.key_claims: Of last sixty patents issued under Declaration of Policy, twenty promptly mortgaged (only one released), sixteen sold outright, twenty-four technically clear but expected to become encumbered. In six-plus years, only one Indian made success handling his own land, and that success could have been made under trust. Does not recall even one case of genuine success. Opposes easy issuance of patents. Advocates making forty acres of each allotment an inalienable homestead. Indians allotted 160 acres each. Knows of no Indian who has more land now than when allotted. Described loan agent inquiry about Billy Hood's patent and agent's attempt to negotiate loan in anticipation of patent. In about 99 out of 100 cases, patent is never asked for until applicant has studied out a plan to alienate it.

testimony.witness_title: Acting Field Clerk, Tahlequah, Oklahoma (Five Civilized Tribes / Cherokee)
testimony.hearing: Response to Field Division letter of April 2, 1921
testimony.committee: Board of Indian Commissioners / Office of Indian Affairs
testimony.subject: Advisability of granting patents-in-fee; outcomes for Five Civilized Tribes Indians
testimony.key_claims: Indiscriminate policy of releasing every Indian of half or less blood degree without supervision is criminally unjust and disastrously impractical. Of those released through competency board, approximately 10% failed completely, 10% barely escape failure, 50% succeeding indifferently, 30% making decided success. Ten percent of those whose restrictions were removed by careful selection sold lands and misused proceeds; remaining 90% made good. Competent Indians rarely apply for removal of restrictions because restricted land is not subject to taxation and they value their homes. Full-blood Indians do not realise value of money. Success correlated with education. Impossible to apply hard and fast rule to all Indians alike. Has worked only with Five Civilized Tribes for six to seven years. Advocates competency board process over indiscriminate release.

testimony.committee: Board of Indian Commissioners / Office of Indian Affairs
testimony.subject: Opposition to rapid release from federal control and indiscriminate citizenship granting
testimony.key_claims: Over 500 Indians on reservation released from government control; very few made good, others sold lands and homes and squandered money, some homeless. Opposed to societies advocating abolition of Indian Bureau. Opposed to granting citizenship in bulk. Contends Department moving too fast in releasing Indians. Advocates competent Indians classifying reservation members in harmony with superintendent, with rigid examination of every Indian regardless of blood or educational status before release. Where Indian has established home, forty acres should be held in trust, nontaxable for given period. Majority of ex-Indian soldiers without lands and not independent citizens. Act of Congress March 2, 1889 provided allotments. American Legion says ex-Indian soldiers should be citizens.

testimony.committee: Board of Indian Commissioners / Office of Indian Affairs
testimony.subject: Criteria for competency; outcomes of patent issuance; reimbursable agreements
testimony.key_claims: Many different ideas of competency exist among superintendents: commercial success, likelihood of running through property, or education. Department has not provided clear guidance; superintendents believe Department desires rapid patent issuance but burden of responsibility falls on superintendent. Several hundred patents granted at reservation; does not believe half dozen of entire number resulted in Indians being as competent as average white man. First generation since allotting ran through more than half land holdings. If land held in trust, Indians have good prospect of becoming worthy citizens; if turned loose most would become parasites. Patents generally theoretically assume patentee has sufficient knowledge and business foresight. Reimbursable plan, if properly handled, would help Indians. Advocates more schooling, mission work, better superintendents. Competent Indian never makes application for removal of restrictions. At competency commission hearings, those who asked for patents were not nearly as qualified as those who did not.
